sources.title: race
sources.scope: Numbered noun/verb entries, usage labels and etymologies
sources.summary: Distinct entries cover lineage/classification and motion/contest/current; the former passes through French and Italian, the latter has a Germanic history. Broader human collective, kind and nonhuman senses also occur.
sources.limit: Historical senses are usage evidence, not scientific endorsement of human taxonomies; reported first dates are not exhaustive corpus searches.

sources.title: is
sources.scope: Verb entry, dialectal labels and etymology; unrelated abbreviation/prefix entries distinguished
sources.summary: Standard is is the third-person singular present indicative of be; dialectal uses broaden that distribution. Cognates include German ist, Latin est and Greek esti.
sources.limit: The separate is-/iso- entry and the English suffix -ist must not be conflated with this verb; grammar requires context beyond an isolated spelling.

sources.title: -ism
sources.scope: Suffix senses 1–3, independent noun and etymology
sources.summary: Suffix senses include act/practice/process, characteristic behavior, attribute-based prejudice/discrimination, state/condition/property and doctrine. The independent noun has a narrower theory/cause/doctrine use. The suffix history passes through French and Latin to Greek formations.
sources.limit: The suffix is not restricted to consciously professed doctrine and is not historically English is plus m. A formed word still needs its attested usage.

sources.title: -ist
sources.summary: The noun-forming suffix marks doers, practitioners, specialists or adherents; an adjective-forming use marks characteristic association. French and Latin forms connect to Greek -istes.
sources.limit: It does not determine a predicate’s truth or permanence and is not derived from the German copula ist.

sources.title: racism
sources.scope: Definitions, usage discussion, First Known Use and etymology
sources.summary: The entry includes racial-essentialist/superiority belief, discriminatory conduct and systemic oppression/advantage. Its First Known Use field gives 1886, but its usage discussion says no apparent pre-twentieth-century instances. Immediate derivation is race plus -ism, possibly influenced by French.
sources.limit: The entry’s dating discrepancy remains unresolved pending actual attestations; the atlas does not silently select one field as a definitive first use.

sources.title: racist
sources.summary: The adjective can describe beliefs, conduct and systemic policies; the noun describes a person through the specified belief/orientation. The word is connected with race and -ist, possibly through French.
sources.limit: Noun and adjective constructions have different scopes; the dictionary does not determine the application to a particular record.

sources.title: -ism
sources.scope: Separate displayed dictionary entries and suffix senses
sources.summary: This treatment includes state of being, process/result, doctrine, characteristic practice and discrimination, corroborating the non-doctrinal range of the suffix.
sources.limit: Several displayed dictionary divisions on one page do not constitute independent historical corpora.

sources.title: race
sources.scope: Returned numbered entries including the ginger-root homograph
sources.summary: A separate root/ginger entry occurs alongside motion and human-group uses. It is retained as a distinct homograph, not as an origin for racism.
sources.limit: The retry did not recover support for the earlier candidate’s radix etymology or obsolete label; those assertions are withdrawn from this entry’s summary, not filled from memory.

sources.title: race, Dictionnaire, ninth edition
sources.scope: French headword, etymology and numbered senses
sources.summary: French rasse is traced to Italian razza; the further connection to Latin generatio through apheresis is tentative. Lineage and historical classification senses remain context-marked.
sources.limit: The proposed further ancestry differs from Treccani’s haraz account; both remain attributed proposals.

sources.title: razza, Vocabolario
sources.summary: Treccani proposes Old French haraz, associated with horse breeding, through resegmentation with an article. It discusses nonhuman classification and problems with historical human classifications.
sources.limit: This is not reconciled with the Académie proposal by an unsupported assertion of consensus.

sources.title: Be
sources.scope: Indexed sections on main/auxiliary be, temporary/permanent conditions, identity and existence
sources.summary: Be can act as a main verb or auxiliary; main-verb uses include temporary and continuing descriptions, group membership and existence. Is belongs to its present paradigm.
sources.limit: The directly opened page was unavailable; indexed primary text is not direct page or grammar-book access.

sources.title: Verbs: types
sources.summary: Linking verbs take nominal, adjectival, adverbial or prepositional complements. Auxiliary be participates in passive and progressive constructions.
sources.limit: Introductory English grammar is not a universal ontology or grammar of all languages; direct page retrieval was unavailable.

sources.title: On Interpretation
sources.summary: Names, verbs, time, combination and assertion are distinguished. Isolated terms do not perform all the work of a truth-evaluable assertion.
sources.limit: The English translation was read, not independently collated Greek or every subsequent theory of the copula.

sources.title: Gender and Race: (What) Are They? (What) Do We Want Them To Be?
sources.scope: Selected pp.32–35, 43–48; diagram on printed p.51 visually inspected
sources.summary: Haslanger distinguishes conceptual, descriptive and analytical inquiry and advances an explicitly revisionary account involving racialization, attributed ancestry and social position. Her race/ethnicity scheme belongs to that project.
sources.limit: Her analytical purpose and definition are not automatically the book author’s descriptive task; selected passages are not a complete critical reading.

sources.title: How to Do Things with Words, Lecture XI
sources.summary: The abstract treats locutionary and illocutionary analysis as aspects of utterances rather than an absolute division between describing and acting.
sources.limit: Lecture text and full felicity conditions remain uninspected; an abstract cannot stand in for the complete speech-act theory.

sources.title: How to Really Do Things with Words: Performance Before the Performative
sources.summary: The abstract distinguishes speaking about, speaking to and logological inquiry into what speaking does, placing ontology and rhetoric in a larger comparison.
sources.limit: Abstract-level orientation only; no complete original-language or translation analysis is claimed.

sources.title: On Concept and Object
sources.limit: The original argument remains a retrieval target. The English publication must not be dated to 1892.

sources.title: The Conservation of Races
sources.scope: Argument on physical criteria, history, collective striving and American belonging
sources.summary: Du Bois disputes the sufficiency of physical classifications and discusses common history, traditions and collective striving, including American and Black belonging together.
sources.limit: Period categories and generalizations are retained as historical text, not presented as current biological science.

sources.title: Rethinking Racism: Toward a Structural Interpretation
sources.summary: The abstract proposes racialized social systems as the organizing basis of structural interpretation instead of reducing racism to individual psychological disposition.
sources.limit: The abstract is not the complete article or the author’s later work.

sources.title: Colonialidad del poder y clasificación social
sources.scope: Original journal Spanish abstract and metadata
sources.summary: The abstract relates racial/ethnic classification to colonial power and capitalism in material and subjective dimensions.
sources.limit: The original Spanish abstract, not the full article, supports this summary; English conceptual synthesis is separately attributed.

sources.title: Understanding racism
sources.scope: Indexed original publisher abstract and metadata
sources.summary: Appiah treats racism centrally as ideology that oppresses racial identities; racialism is essentialism about those identities. His account distinguishes false racialism, morally impermissible attitudes and differential treatment.
sources.limit: This is not his separate 1990 chapter Racisms. The complete 2024 article was not independently retrieved; an opponent’s paraphrase cannot supply its unread argument.

sources.title: Moral status of believing in races
sources.scope: Indexed original publisher abstract and selected opening argument
sources.summary: Webster agrees with central ideology/oppression claims while arguing that belief in racial essences is morally problematic through stereotyping that undermines agency.
sources.limit: The disputed belief is not every recognition of socially real identity. Indexed selected text is not direct complete-article inspection; the title is not an editorial paraphrase of its thesis.

sources.title: Racism, Moralism, and Social Criticism
sources.summary: Social criticism involves empirical and normative inquiry and should not be confined to assessments of individual moral character.
sources.limit: This is not Shelby’s 2002 response to Garcia; the complete 2014 argument and its interlocutors remain separate.

sources.authority: Michael Omi and Howard Winant; Routledge
sources.title: Racial Formation in the United States, third edition
sources.summary: The publisher describes historical formation and transformation of racial meanings, identities and institutions.
sources.limit: A synopsis is not an inspected chapter or a reconstruction of the authors’ full theory.

sources.title: The Heart of Racism
sources.limit: Full original argument not retrieved; do not reconstruct it through an opponent’s account.

sources.title: Is Racism in the “Heart”?
sources.limit: The interrupted candidate incorrectly named The Philosophical Forum. Keep this text distinct from the 2014 article; no unread argument is summarized.

sources.title: Putting Racism Back in the Head
sources.version: 2025; online 29 April; reference-order correction noted 15 July 2025
sources.summary: Scott defends a bias-centered epistemic account of personal racism, separating the number/significance of truth-distorting attitudes from other properties. His concluding comparison distinguishes norms for people from functional outcomes of institutions or algorithms.
sources.limit: An explicit rival account, not a consensus definition or a denial that non-personal racism can exist. No numerical scale for this book is imported.

sources.title: Epistemic Injustice: Power and the Ethics of Knowing
sources.summary: Testimonial and hermeneutical injustice concern persons as knowers and relations among knowledge practices, stereotypes and social power.
sources.limit: The abstract is not the full book or a diagnosis of a particular exchange.

sources.title: Tracking Epistemic Violence, Tracking Practices of Silencing
sources.summary: The abstract examines hearer failure through pernicious ignorance to meet a speaker’s dependence and vulnerability in communication.
sources.limit: The full taxonomy of silencing was not retrieved; it does not license equating every silence with the same injustice.

sources.title: Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex
sources.version: University of Chicago Legal Forum, 1989, article 8
sources.scope: Original journal landing metadata; full paper not inspected in retry
sources.limit: Full paper remains a primary-text target. No substantive argument is inferred merely from title or influence.

sources.title: Declaration on Race and Racial Prejudice
sources.summary: Equal dignity is joined to recognition of difference and cultural identity. The account of racism includes ideologies, attitudes, conduct and structural/institutional practices producing inequality.
sources.limit: A declaration is neither a case judgment nor interchangeable with a treaty or domestic cause of action.

sources.title: International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination
sources.version: Adopted 1965; opened for signature 1966; entered into force 1969
sources.scope: English Articles 1–7; Article 1 visually inspected on printed p.216
sources.summary: Article 1 specifies distinctions, exclusions, restrictions or preferences, protected grounds and purpose/effect concerning equal rights. Adjacent citizenship/nationality and special-measure provisions remain part of the definition’s context.
sources.limit: Domestic application, reservations and remedies need their own sources; racial discrimination and racism are not automatically identical headwords.

sources.authority: Gay McDougall; UN Audiovisual Library of International Law
sources.title: Introductory note on ICERD
sources.summary: The note explains the treaty’s development, effects-based discrimination and interpretation of protected grounds.
sources.limit: Named expert commentary is not treaty wording, a court judgment or a current national-implementation audit.

sources.title: ECRI Glossary
sources.scope: Race, racism, racialisation, direct/indirect/structural discrimination and incident entries
sources.summary: The racism entry emphasizes a belief justifying contempt or superiority on specified grounds. Neighboring entries separately describe discriminatory operations, structures and incident recording.
sources.limit: The belief entry does not deny structures that the glossary separately defines; recording a perceived incident is not itself a criminal adjudication.

sources.title: United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
sources.scope: Articles 8–9, 13 and 33, official text hosted by UNHCR
sources.summary: These provisions concern forced assimilation, culture, names/languages, community belonging and collective authority over identity/membership alongside citizenship.
sources.limit: Indigenous peoples’ particular collective rights are not a generic race checkbox or proof of an individual’s membership.

sources.authority: U.S. Congress; text hosted by EEOC
sources.title: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended
sources.summary: The employment statute distinguishes treatment, disparate-impact and motivating-factor provisions, with different operative requirements and defenses.
sources.limit: U.S. employment law is not a universal definition or an automatically applicable rule for another setting.

sources.authority: American Association of Physical Anthropologists; now AABA
sources.title: Statement on Race and Racism
sources.version: Adopted 27 March 2019 under the former association name
sources.scope: Statement on human variation, social race and embodied consequences
sources.summary: The statement rejects discrete biological racial divisions as an adequate representation of human variation while affirming the social reality and embodied consequences of racial organization.
sources.limit: Biological non-discreteness does not erase social identity; the statement does not assign anyone a personal identity.

sources.authority: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
sources.title: Using Population Descriptors in Genetics and Genomics Research
sources.summary: Descriptors should match research questions; race should not proxy for genetic variation, and self-identification, ancestry and relevant exposures should be distinguished.
sources.limit: Selected recommendations, not the whole report; these do not direct removal of racial identity from social inquiry.

sources.authority: U.S. Office of Management and Budget
sources.title: 2024 Statistical Policy Directive No.15
sources.summary: Federal race/ethnicity categories are sociopolitical, not biological/genetic constructs, and statistical standards are distinguished from eligibility determinations.
sources.limit: Agency implementation and transition dates remain separately unverified; no universal current deadline is asserted.

sources.title: Levels of Racism: A Theoretic Framework and a Gardener’s Tale
sources.version: American Journal of Public Health 90(8), 2000, pp.1212–1215
sources.scope: PMC abstract; full PDF not read
sources.summary: The abstract introduces institutionalized, personally mediated and internalized levels as a theoretical framework.
sources.limit: The more detailed statements used here come from the separately retrieved direct interview, not an invented full-paper reading.

sources.title: Camara Jones on racism
sources.version: Page displays 22 July 2016; URL bears a later date
sources.scope: Direct answers on definition and three levels
sources.summary: Jones discusses opportunity/value structures, personally mediated assumptions/actions and internalization, including omissions, unintentional conduct and institutional operation without an identifiable individual perpetrator.
sources.limit: This attributed framework is not a particular-case finding or evidence that all authorities agree on the same definition.

senses.text: Lineage and human classification, with distinct historical uses.
Human collective or broad kind, not only a subdivision.
Movement, contest, course or current with a distinct word history.
A separate ginger-root homograph; no ancestry of racism inferred.
Historical identity and social classification; frameworks remain attributed.
A purpose-bound administrative category, not an entire identity.
Standard third-person singular present of be.
A property or condition predicated through a complement.
An identifying construction can link descriptions of one referent.
Existential construction, often with there.
Locative or situational complementation.
Auxiliary in progressive/passive constructions.
Action, practice, process or behavior.
Condition, state, property or result.
Doctrine or system, not the suffix’s sole range.
Discriminatory practice/orientation in applicable formed words.
Doer, practitioner or specialist.
An adherent or participant in a school/orientation.
Adjectival characteristic association.
Belief-centered definitions have specified objects and criteria.
Conduct and omissions in specified frameworks.
Racialized systems, institutions and distributions.
Ideological accounts and explicit philosophical disputes.
Internalization within Jones’s framework.
Adjective predicate whose subject and scope must be retained.
Person-category with context-dependent application.
Neighboring legal category, not a synonym by stipulation.
Difference, identity and belonging alongside equal dignity.
Reception as a knower is a distinct relation.

relations.statement: Literary relation does not require shared word ancestry.
The root entry is a distinct homograph.
The dictionary names race and -ism as immediate elements.
Process/practice senses are available; whole-word use supplies particular meaning.
Condition is a suffix sense; structural theory needs separate support.
The dictionary relates racist to race and -ist.
A nominal category differs from an act-predicate.
An adjective need not have a person as its subject.
Semantic connections between being and condition do not establish common etymology.
German ist is cognate with is, not the source of English -ist.
Property predication and referential identification are not interchangeable.
Existence and attribution do different work.
Passive/progressive auxiliaries do not declare enduring essence.
Subject, time and context locate a predicate; grammar does not verify it.
Act-description and person-categorization differ in referent and possible uptake.
Belief and structure accounts have different units of analysis.
Appiah/Webster disagree on the moral status of racialist belief.
A social description and a legally actionable category require distinct records.
Collection categories need not exhaust personal or community identity.
Social construction can coexist with real identity and equal dignity.
Identity and knowledge reception can be examined without ranking credibility by identity.
Classification and structures develop together in attributed historical accounts.
Shared humanity and group belonging need not occupy the same scale.
Self-description, community membership and administrative coding have different authorities.
Description enters an exchange with reception and practical effects.

disagreements.account: The tentative generatio and haraz accounts are retained as competing proposals, not resolved by prestige.
The 1886 First Known Use field and no apparent pre-twentieth-century examples in the usage discussion require attestation-level checking.
ECRI assigns structures a separate entry; its belief-centered racism entry does not deny structural discrimination.
Webster disputes the moral separation of false racial essentialism in Appiah’s account; social self-identification is not thereby equated with essentialism.
Lexical description and concept revision answer different questions; neither silently replaces RF-01.
Non-discrete biological variation does not remove social identities, and a statistical category is not a genetic population.
Declarations, treaty text, glossary and employment statute have different reach and criteria.

Scott defends an epistemic bias account of personal racism against moral and socio-political rivals; his account also distinguishes non-personal entities. This is disagreement, not a universal replacement definition.
